doc.title: John Pizzarelli interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 18, 2023 [interview 2 of 2]

title: James Taylor's standards record and working together on guitar
summary: About seventeen years later Taylor invited him to help on a standards record. They worked out finger-picked arrangements, and he added rhythm guitar to each tune.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Goldings played piano and Steve Gadd was the drummer. And I remember when I played the track for Bucky, I said, “Hey listen to this.” So he heard the thing and then the second he heard [sings] the first chunk he said, “Who’s the rhythm player?” I said, “Thank you very much.” I said, I passed the test. So James said something to me like, “Well you’ve got to show me how you do that rhythm thing, that’s really great.” I mean he really liked the rhythm guitar. And I said to him, “Well you can show me that finger picking thing and we’ll be even” you know. So when he — we had to do not “I’ll be Home for Christmas,” the other one. “Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas.” Same date. But he had a lead sheet of the verse. [sings] Christmas future is far away/Christmas past is past/Christmas present is here to stay. And so there was the thing and I did a Bucky Pizzarelli thing. And I looked at the lead sheet and I said it says there’s an A chord, whatever the hell it was, the third was in the bass. Because Bucky would always say, “Look at the lead sheet and see where the bass notes are, it’s going to show you all your voice leading is going to be right there.” So if you just played A – E – A – E — it wasn’t A – E, it was a chromatic movement down [scats] and I could see the whole thing and I was so proud of myself because I was like — I finally — it was another moment, another Bucky Pizzarelli moment. And so James called me, so it only took him twenty-some-odd years before — no, about seventeen years later he texted me and said, “I want to do a record of standards and you da man” it said. And he just wanted me to come in, and I think the original idea was for me to be there and make sure harmonically he was in the right ballpark. And then, because the first thing he did was “Old Man River.” He had some really nice things on that. And I was like, “Well there’s a nice little chord you could play here,” and he’d go, “okay.” And I was in the booth and then after that he said, “well let’s” — we had played together “My Blue Heaven” just on a gig that we did shortly after the record in ’01. And I said, “Let’s play ‘My Blue Heaven.’” And he said — we started to play it, the two guitars together, I was sort of finger picking and he was finger picking but I was sort of coming up with different inversions around what he was doing. And I had the bass note on the seven string classical that I had. And then he was sort of like, “Well that’s pretty good.” He goes, “You want to put rhythm on that now?” And I said sure. So they run it back and I had an L 7 and I was — I played the rhythm on it and he was like, “Yeah.” So then we had a format when we’d do “Pennies From Heaven” he would come up with his thing, and he always wanted to change the chords on the second time around so we would come up with the different set of — this was like over — each tune would be like six hours. But then at the end he’d go, “Hey, put the rhythm on now.” He’d get all excited, “Get the rhythm.” And I’d get the rhythm out. So he just had a — and he just James Taylorized everything. He made it all his own thing. Paul was more like — what Paul said, it was difficult for him and he goes, you know I’m only trying to

sing like Little Richard or Elvis when I sing rock & roll. But here I am singing standards. I don’t know who to sing like. And it was really cool. So with James Taylor he knew it was going to be James Taylorized. He just wanted to make sure it was within — you know he really had a — he was really smart. They both were smart, I mean they are both geniuses in their own little way.
